ev.out-of-africa.t: Modern humans had left Africa before, as early as 125,000 years ago, but those groups left no trace in living people. The dispersal that lasted set out from East Africa roughly 70,000–50,000 years ago, crossed to Arabia, followed the coasts to South Asia before 55,000 years ago and reached Oceania by about 50,000 years ago.
ev.sahul.t: People crossed the straits of Wallacea into Sahul, the joined landmass of New Guinea and Australia, around 65,000–50,000 years ago; the oldest settlement evidence is given as 50,000–60,000 years and the oldest human remains as about 40,000 years. It was the first ocean crossing of our species.
ev.sapiens-europe.t: Modern humans spread across Europe about 40,000 years ago, certainly after 40,000 and possibly as early as 43,000 years ago, entering from the Levant through the Balkans and the Danube corridor. The Neanderthals vanished within a few thousand years of their arrival.
ev.peopling-americas.t: Beringia stood dry from about 30,000 years ago, and people lived on it through the glacial maximum. The Americas were occupied no later than 14,000 years ago and possibly before 20,000; Monte Verde in Chile is dated about 14,500 years, the Clovis points to 13,250–12,800 years, and footprints at White Sands may be 21,000–23,000 years old. The ice-free corridor opened only about 13,800 years ago, so the first road was probably the Pacific coast.
ev.first-dogs.t: The dog is domesticated in Siberia about 23,000 years ago.
ev.first-pottery.t: The earliest pottery is made in China between about 20,000 and 16,000 years ago, long before farming.
ev.monte-verde.t: On a creek near Puerto Montt in southern Chile, people build about twelve huts of wood and hide around 14,500 years ago, butcher mastodon-like Notiomastodon, gather nine kinds of seaweed and some 45 food plants, and leave a footprint. Tom Dillehay’s excavations from 1977 undermined the idea that the Clovis people came first; a 2026 study disputes the date and Dillehay contests it.
ev.clovis.t: The Clovis culture spreads across North America, from southern Canada to northern Mexico, about 13,050–12,750 years ago. Its fluted stone points, named from Blackwater Draw near Clovis, New Mexico, tip the spears of mammoth and bison hunters; the genome of the Anzick child, buried in Montana with Clovis tools, ties them to today’s Native Americans.
ev.first-farming.n: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
ev.first-farming.t: Agriculture begins in the Fertile Crescent between about 10,000 and 9000 BC; sheep, then goats and cattle, are domesticated in South-west Asia in the same millennium.
ev.gobekli-tepe.t: Hunter-gatherers raise great circular enclosures of carved T-shaped pillars on a hilltop near Şanlıurfa from about 9500 BC: foxes, boars, snakes and vultures are cut in the stone, and nearly 200 pillars may stand in at least 20 enclosures. Excavated by Klaus Schmidt from 1995, it is among the first monumental architecture made by human hands, perhaps older than farming itself.
ev.jericho.t: Natufian hunters camp at the spring of Jericho around 10,000 BC and the first permanent settlement grows there between 9500 and 9000 BC. Around 8000 BC its people build a stone wall over 3.6 m high and a tower over 8.5 m high with 22 steps inside; in the later town, founded around 6800 BC, they plaster and paint the skulls of their dead.
ev.rice.t: Rice is domesticated in China between about 9000 and 6000 BC; by 5000 BC the Hemudu culture grows it in eastern China.
ev.potato.t: The potato is domesticated between about 8000 and 5000 BC in southern Peru and north-western Bolivia, around Lake Titicaca.
ev.catalhoyuk.t: Çatalhöyük on the Konya plain flourishes around 7000 BC: houses packed wall to wall, entered by ladders through the roofs, which serve as streets. Its people paint murals and make more than 2,500 clay figurines; recent work puts the population at 600–800 in an average year, far below the early guesses of 5,000–7,000.
ev.maize.t: Maize is domesticated from the wild grass teosinte in southern Mexico, probably in the Balsas valley, about 9,000 years ago, and only once. It reaches highland Ecuador by 8,000 years ago; the oldest cobs, from Guilá Naquitz in Oaxaca, are about 6,250 years old.
ev.anatolian-farmers.t: Farming came to Europe with people, not only with ideas: from about 7000 BC Anatolian farmers moved through south-eastern Europe, up the Danube with the Linear Pottery culture and along the Mediterranean with Cardial Ware, and reached Britain by a mass migration about 4000 BC. Hadrian’s Wall, raised in AD 122, cut across an island whose people had shared this migration for four thousand years; ancient DNA finds Britain’s real genetic frontier a thousand years older than the Wall, in Bronze Age migrants who raised farmer ancestry in England and Wales between 1000 and 875 BC but barely in Scotland (Patterson et al. 2021).
ev.the-sail.t: Pottery from Mesopotamia shows boats with sails around 5500 BC; ancient Egypt follows.
ev.eridu-uruk.t: Around 5400 BC the Ubaid people at Eridu in southern Iraq begin to farm grain in the arid south, and Uruk is founded around 5000 BC; the Choga Mami canals irrigate fields around 4700 BC.
ev.copper-smelting.t: The Vinča culture of the Balkans makes the earliest known copper smelting of the Old World; the timeline of inventions dates it to about 5000 BC in Serbia.
ev.nabta-playa.n: The stone circle of Nabta Playa
ev.nabta-playa.t: Herders at Nabta Playa in the Egyptian desert raise stone circles aligned to the summer solstice around 4800 BC.
ev.huaca-prieta.t: Maize is farmed at Huaca Prieta on the north coast of Peru around 4700 BC, and the earliest known dyed cotton cloth, about 6,000 years old, is woven there.
ev.varna-gold.t: The Varna culture of Bulgaria, from about 4600 to 4200 BC, buries its chiefs in graves of gold and shows the first signs of kingship.
ev.arnhem-rock-art.t: Around 4000 BC the rock painters of Arnhem Land in northern Australia depict skirmishes between groups.
ev.bronze-arslantepe.t: Bronze smelting begins in the fourth millennium BC; the Maykop culture of the Caucasus, of 3700–3000 BC, may be its origin, and the earliest bronze swords, of arsenical bronze, come from Arslantepe in Anatolia around 3300 BC.
ev.silk-3630.t: Silk garments are made in China by 3630 BC.
ev.ggantija.t: The megalithic temples of Ġgantija on Gozo, in Malta, are begun around 3600 BC.
ev.norte-chico-3600.t: The Norte Chico civilisation of northern Peru begins around 3600 BC; large-scale settlement and communal building start at Caral-Supe around 3100 BC, and the oldest adobe building of the Americas is raised in Peru.
ev.botai-horses.t: Horses are probably domesticated on the Eurasian steppe around 3500 BC; the Botai culture of northern Kazakhstan has the evidence.
ev.sahara-dries.t: Around 3500 BC the drying of the Sahara spurs the Neolithic of the Sahel; in Egypt the dead are already being mummified at Nekhen.
ev.wheel.t: Evidence of the wheel appears between about 4000 and 3400 BC in Ukraine, Poland and Germany. The oldest wooden wheel yet found, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, is about 5,150 years old; the potter’s wheel is in use in Mesopotamia by 3250 BC.
ev.otzi.t: Ötzi dies in the Ötztal Alps around 3300 BC, it is believed by homicide.
ev.yamnaya.t: Herders with wagons and horses spread from the Don–Volga steppe about 3400–3200 BC. Around 2500 BC their descendants reached central Europe as the Corded Ware culture, the Altai as the Afanasievo culture and, with the Bell Beaker complex, Britain. The migration is the leading explanation for the spread of the Indo-European languages.
ev.writing-sumer.n: Writing begins in Sumer and Egypt
ev.writing-sumer.t: Cuneiform and hieroglyphs are first used in the late fourth millennium BC, at Uruk and in the Nile valley.
ev.egypt-first-dynasty.t: About 3100 BC the Nile valley comes under one court; the First Dynasty begins.
ev.camels-3000.t: Camels are domesticated around 3000 BC, and the first agriculture appears in North Africa.
ev.cycladic.t: The Cycladic civilisation and the Aegean Bronze Age begin around 3000 BC; the marble Harp Player of Keros is made around 2800–2700 BC.
ev.jawa-dam.t: Jawa in the Jordanian desert is founded around 3000 BC with the world’s first known dam.
ev.liangzhu.t: Before 3000 BC the Liangzhu culture of the lower Yangtze carves deity images on jade cong. Near Eastern grains appear in China around 3000 BC and the potter’s wheel is in use there in the third millennium BC.
ev.shekel.t: The shekel is introduced in Mesopotamia as a unit of weight and money; the Sumerians build cities and work metals, and gold comes into use in the Middle East.
ev.stonehenge-3000.t: Stonehenge is begun around 3000 BC: its first phase is a ditch and bank with 56 wooden posts. Newgrange in Ireland is built between about 3000 and 2500 BC.
ev.sydney-engravings.t: The rock engravings of the Sydney region date from around 3000 BC.
ev.valdivia-pottery.n: The first pottery of the Americas
ev.valdivia-pottery.t: The first pottery of the Americas is made in what is now Ecuador in the third millennium BC, while settled villages spread through Mesoamerica.
ev.bantu.t: Between about 4000 BC and AD 500 Bantu-speaking farmers spread from the Cameroon–Nigeria highlands across a third of Africa. The western stream reached the southern edge of the rainforest about 500 BC; the eastern stream stood west of Lake Victoria by 500 BC, on the Kenyan and Tanzanian coast by 100 BC–AD 300, in KwaZulu-Natal by about AD 300 and in Limpopo by about AD 500.
ev.austronesians.t: Around 3000–1500 BC farmers with outrigger canoes and sails left Taiwan for Luzon, then the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi and the Marianas by 1500 BC. The Lapita people carried the expansion to Melanesia by 1200 BC and to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa about 900–800 BC; after a long pause their descendants reached Tahiti by 700, Hawai‘i by 900, Rapa Nui by 1000 and New Zealand about 1250. It was the widest dispersal of any people before the modern age.
ev.troy-2920.t: By Manfred Korfmann’s reading of the excavations, Troy is founded around 2920 BC.
ev.eshnunna-statues.t: The wide-eyed votive statues of the Square Temple at Eshnunna are made around 2900 BC, as the Early Dynastic period of Sumer begins.
ev.mari-2900.t: The first kingdom of Mari on the Euphrates is founded around 2900 BC.
ev.phonograms.t: From about 2900 BC Sumerian pictographs evolve into phonograms, signs for sounds; the first Akkadian names are recorded around 2890 BC.
ev.egypt-second-dynasty.t: Hotepsekhemwy begins Egypt’s Second Dynasty around 2890 BC, and wars divide the kingdom from 2775 to 2650 BC.
ev.hong-bang.t: By Vietnamese tradition Kinh Dương Vương founds the Hồng Bàng dynasty and the kingdom of Xích Quỷ in 2879 BC.
ev.egypt-calendar.t: Egypt installs a calendar of 365 days around 2874 BC.
ev.methuselah-tree.t: A bristlecone pine germinates in the White Mountains of California around 2832 BC: the Methuselah tree.
ev.elam-2800.t: The kingdom of Elam is created in south-western Iran around 2800–2700 BC.
ev.harappan-2800.t: The Harappan 2 phase of the Indus valley, around 2800–2600 BC, leads to the unified Indus civilisation of about 2600 BC.
ev.kalibangan-plough.t: A ploughed field at Kalibangan in the Indus valley is dated to about 2800 BC; the first ploughs had been made in Europe by 3500 BC.
ev.keros-harp.t: A Cycladic sculptor carves the marble Seated Harp Player of Keros around 2800–2700 BC.
ev.cucuteni-end.t: The Cucuteni–Trypillia culture of Romania, Moldova and south-western Ukraine ends around 2750 BC.
ev.khasekhemwy.t: The first Egyptian statuary, shale and limestone figures of King Khasekhemwy, is made at Nekhen around 2700 BC.
ev.yellow-emperor.t: Chinese tradition dates the mythical reign of the Yellow Emperor from about 2698 BC; the age of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors is counted from 2852 BC.
ev.djoser.t: Imhotep builds the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara in the twenty-seventh century BC, Egypt’s earliest building of stone.
ev.sinai-mines.t: Egypt develops copper mines and turquoise quarries in Sinai under Sneferu and Khufu; the earliest African picture of ploughing is painted in the tomb of Itet and Nefermaat at Meidum.
ev.sneferu.t: Sneferu’s armies bring back about 7,000 prisoners from Nubia and 11,000 prisoners and 13,100 cattle from Libya; he sends 40 ships to Byblos for cedar, and copper and turquoise are mined in Sinai.
ev.gilgamesh-king.t: The semi-legendary Gilgamesh is supposed to reign at Uruk around 2650 BC; Nippur keeps a bronze bar that defines the cubit.
ev.kalibangan-2650.t: The Harappan town of Kalibangan is abandoned around 2650 BC as the Ghaggar river dries; at Dholavira reservoirs, script, metals and pottery are in use.
ev.indus-cities.t: The mature Harappan phase begins about 2600 BC; the Indus civilisation ends about 1700 BC.
ev.caral.t: Caral in Peru’s Supe valley is inhabited from about 2600 to 2000 BC, its temple pyramid 150 m long and 28 m high. With some 3,000 people, and perhaps 20,000 across the nineteen other temple sites of the valley, its excavators call it the oldest urban centre of the Americas; a knotted cord found there may be a quipu.
ev.early-minoan.t: The Early Minoan I period of Crete runs from about 2600 to 2400 BC.
ev.los-millares.t: The Copper Age settlements of Los Millares and Zambujal are founded in Iberia around 2600 BC.
ev.shuruppak.t: The Instructions of Shuruppak, among the earliest known literary texts, are composed in Sumer in 2600–2500 BC.
ev.ur-royal-cemetery.t: The Royal Cemetery of Ur is built in the twenty-sixth century BC; under Mesannepada, from about 2560 BC, Ur grows into a major capital.
ev.great-pyramid-2551.t: Khufu reigns from about 2551 to 2526 BC and builds the Great Pyramid of Giza; his son Khafre adds his pyramid and the Great Sphinx. Djedefre is the first pharaoh to call himself Son of Ra.
ev.lagash-umma.n: The war of Lagash and Umma
ev.lagash-umma.t: The border dispute between Lagash and Umma begins around 2550 BC, under Mesilim of Kish.
ev.assyria-2500.t: Assyria is established around 2500 BC; archaeology shows the site of Assur occupied by 2400 BC.
ev.donkey-chariots.t: The Sumerians harness domestic donkeys to war chariots in the twenty-fifth century BC.
ev.ebla-tablets.t: The archive of Ebla in Syria is written between about 2500 and 2250 BC, while scribal schools flourish in Sumer.
ev.hal-saflieni.t: Work on the underground Hypogeum of Ħal Saflieni in Malta begins around 2500 BC.
ev.hoting-ski.t: The earliest surviving ski is left in a bog at Hoting in Sweden in the twenty-fifth century BC.
ev.khafre-2500.t: The pyramid of Khafre is built at Giza around 2500 BC, with the seated statue Khafre Enthroned. In the next dynasty the Seated Scribe is carved at Saqqara.
ev.mohenjo-daro.t: Mohenjo-daro grows to about 18 km² and 20,000–50,000 people between 2500 and 2000 BC. The Indus civilisation at its peak covers about 480,000 km².
ev.peru-coast-2500.n: The fishing towns of the Peruvian coast
ev.peru-coast-2500.t: Around 2500 BC the people of the Peruvian coast live on fish and mussels, and long-distance trade routes cross South America.
ev.rice-malaysia.t: Rice is first introduced to Malaysia around 2500 BC.
ev.skara-brae.t: Skara Brae in Orkney is abandoned around 2500 BC after about 600 years of occupation.
ev.beaker-britain.t: The people who had raised Stonehenge were almost wholly replaced: between about 2400 and 2000 BC over 90% of British ancestry was overturned by newcomers from the Continent carrying steppe ancestry. The Beaker pots travelled as a fashion in Iberia but as a people in Britain.
ev.egypt-couriers.t: Egypt gives the first official mention of beekeeping and the first documented courier service for written documents in the twenty-fourth century BC.
ev.stonehenge-2400.t: Stonehenge is built between about 2400 and 2200 BC, as the megalithic culture spreads through Europe and the western Mediterranean.
ev.written-akkadian.t: The first written Akkadian, the Semitic language of Sargon’s empire, survives from the twenty-fourth century BC.
ev.hekla-4.t: Hekla in Iceland erupts around 2360 BC, the eruption known as Hekla 4.
ev.lugalzagesi.t: Lugal-Zage-Si of Umma conquers Gu-Edin and unites Sumer around 2350 BC; Mari is destroyed for the first time.
ev.egypt-sixth-dynasty.t: Unas, the last king of the Fifth Dynasty, dies around 2345 BC and the Sixth Dynasty begins with Teti.
ev.akkad.t: Sargon unites the cities of Sumer and Akkad and marches to the Mediterranean; the empire is founded in the late twenty-fourth century BC.
ev.gojoseon.t: Korean myth has Dangun found Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, in 2333 BC.
ev.bahr-yusuf.t: Egyptians widen a branch of the Nile into the Bahr Yusuf canal to Lake Moeris around 2300 BC.
ev.unetice.t: The Únětice culture emerges in today’s Czech Republic around 2300 BC, as metals come into use in northern Europe.
ev.enheduanna.t: Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon-god Nanna at Ur, is born around 2285 BC; her alabaster disc is made there.
ev.naram-sin-stela.t: The victory stela of Naram-Sin of Akkad is carved around 2254–2218 BC, probably at Sippar; it is later carried off to Susa.
ev.maize-southwest.t: Maize, domesticated in southern Mexico, is cultivated in Central America by around 2250 BC, and its farming begins in New Mexico and Arizona about 4,100 years ago.
ev.akkad-largest.t: Around 2240 BC Akkad passes Memphis as the largest city in the world.
ev.india-australia.t: By one estimate migrants from India reach Australia around 2218 BC and mix with the Indigenous Australians.
ev.akkad-falls.t: Nomads invade Akkad from 2217 to 2193 BC, and around 2180 BC the Akkadian Empire falls to the Gutians.
ev.batanes-2200.t: Austronesian seafarers reach the Batanes Islands of the northern Philippines around 2200 BC.
ev.iron-smelting.t: Iron is smelted at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Anatolia between about 2200 and 2000 BC.
ev.kiloyear-event.t: From about 2200 to 2100 BC a great aridification, the 4.2-kiloyear event, strikes Africa and Asia, and the states of the Old World collapse.
ev.old-kingdom-ends.n: The end of the Old Kingdom
ev.old-kingdom-ends.t: Pepi II may die around 2184 BC after the longest reign in history, 94 years. By 2181 BC the Old Kingdom of Egypt has ended and the First Intermediate Period begins.
ev.lagash-2150.t: The city-state of Lagash is re-established around 2150 BC, while the Gutians hold Akkad; the Middle Minoan period begins on Crete around 2160 BC.
ev.gudea.t: Gudea rules Lagash from about 2144 to 2124 BC; his votive statues survive.
ev.ur-iii.t: Ur-Nammu campaigns across Sumer from 2112 BC and founds the Third Dynasty of Ur; the Ziggurat of Ur is built. In 2004 BC the Elamites sack Ur and the dynasty ends.
ev.gilgamesh.t: The Sumerian epic poems, Gilgamesh among them, are written between about 2100 and 2000 BC; an Akkadian version follows.
ev.shahr-e-sukhteh.t: Shahr-e Sukhteh, the Burnt City of eastern Persia, is abandoned in the twenty-first century BC.
ev.sintashta.t: The Sintashta culture emerges on the northern Eurasian steppe around 2100 BC.
ev.stonehenge-bluestones.t: The inner bluestone circles of Stonehenge are raised in the twenty-first century BC. Seahenge, on the Norfolk shore, is built in the late spring of 2049 BC.
ev.xia-2070.n: Yu the Great and the Xia
ev.xia-2070.t: By tradition Yu the Great founds the Xia dynasty in China around 2070 BC; a great flood in the Jishi gorge around 1920 BC may lie behind the legend.
ev.kerma-2050.t: The Middle Kerma culture begins in Upper Nubia around 2050 BC.
ev.middle-kingdom.t: Mentuhotep II of Thebes completes the reunification of Egypt around 2040 BC, and the Middle Kingdom begins.
ev.ban-chiang.t: Early bronze objects at Ban Chiang in Thailand date from around 2000 BC, from a society without cities or armies.
ev.capacha.t: The Capacha culture begins in Colima, in western Mexico, around 2000 BC, and people settle at Matanchén in Nayarit.
ev.glass-2000.t: Glass appears around 2000 BC, and Old Assyrian cuneiform evolves from the Sumerian.
ev.kenya-herders.t: Farmers and herders settle in what is now Kenya around 2000 BC, and the ancestors of the Latins arrive in Italy.
ev.last-mammoths.t: The last woolly mammoths die out on Wrangel Island in the Arctic around 2000 BC, centuries after the pyramids of Giza were built.
ev.indo-aryans.t: From the Sintashta (c. 2200–1900 BC) and Andronovo (2000–1450 BC) cultures of the steppe, Indo-Aryan speakers moved south through the Bactria–Margiana oasis towns and in several waves into the Punjab, about 1900 and 1700–1400 BC. The Rigveda, their earliest text, is placed about 1500–1200 BC.
ev.egypt-12th.t: Amenemhat I founds the Twelfth Dynasty around 1995 BC. Senusret I conquers Lower Nubia to the Second Cataract in 1953 BC, and war with Nubia follows in 1913–1903 BC.
ev.leubingen.t: A chieftain, the King of Leubingen, is buried in Thuringia in 1942 BC under a stone cairn 20 m across.
ev.jishi-flood.t: A great flood bursts from the Jishi gorge on the upper Yellow River around 1920 BC; it may be linked with the founding of the Xia dynasty.
ev.cacao-1900.t: Around 1900 BC the Mokaya of the Pacific coast of Chiapas, in Mexico, are preparing drinks of cacao.
ev.lothal-1900.t: The late Harappan phase of the Indus civilisation begins around 1900 BC, and its port of Lothal in Gujarat is abandoned.
ev.minoan-palaces-1900.t: The Old Palace period of Minoan Crete begins around 1900 BC, and the palace at Knossos rises.
ev.sumer-ends-1900.t: The last Sumerian dynasty falls around 1900 BC; the Amorite Shamshi-Adad I founds a kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia around 1808 BC.
ev.senusret-1860.t: Senusret III of Egypt’s Middle Kingdom inspects the Nubian frontier around 1860 BC and leads four punitive campaigns south. A head of him is now at the Nelson-Atkins Museum.
ev.proto-sinaitic.t: The first alphabet, the Proto-Sinaitic script, appears in Egypt around 1850 BC.
ev.kahun-papyrus.t: The Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus, written around 1825 BC at el-Lahun, is the oldest known Egyptian medical text.
ev.hyksos-avaris.t: From about 1800 BC the Hyksos settle in the Nile delta with their capital at Avaris, and by about 1750 BC they hold northern Egypt.
ev.maya-villages-1800.t: Settled Maya communities form in Mesoamerica around 1800 BC.
ev.nordic-bronze.t: The Nordic Bronze Age begins in Scandinavia around 1800 BC.
ev.troy-vi.t: The sixth city of Troy flourishes for five centuries, from about 1800 to 1300 BC.
ev.hammurabi-code.t: The oldest record of Hammurabi's law code dates to about 1780 BC.
ev.mari-1757.t: Hammurabi of Babylon sacks Mari in 1757 BC and destroys the palace of its king Zimri-Lim.
ev.veniaminof.t: Mount Veniaminof on the Alaska Peninsula erupts colossally around 1750 BC.
ev.indus-ends-1700.n: The end of the Indus cities
ev.indus-ends-1700.t: The Indus Valley civilisation declines from about 1800 BC and ends around 1700 BC; the Cemetery H culture carries it on.
ev.minoan-new-palaces.t: Around 1700 BC the Old Palace period of Crete ends and the second palaces are built; Aegean metalworkers now make ornaments to rival the Near East’s jewellers.
ev.leavened-bread.t: Leavened bread is developed in Egypt around 1680 BC.
ev.hyksos-memphis.t: Around 1650 BC the Hyksos take Memphis; Egypt’s 13th and 14th dynasties collapse and the Hyksos 15th dynasty rules the north.
ev.mingtiao.t: By tradition Tang of Shang overthrows Jie, the last king of Xia, at the battle of Mingtiao around 1646 BC or earlier, and establishes the Shang dynasty.
ev.cooling-1627.t: Tree rings across the world record a cooling of several years from 1627 BC, possibly from volcanic eruptions.
ev.thera.t: The Minoan eruption buries Akrotiri about 1600 BC.
ev.shang.t: The Shang rule the Yellow River plain from about 1600 BC until the Zhou overthrow the last Shang king about 1046 BC.
ev.el-morro-tulcan.t: A pyramid is raised at El Morro del Tulcán, at today’s Popayán in Colombia, around 1600 BC.
ev.mycenae-1550.t: Early Mycenaean culture, with its weapons, Cyclopean walls and chariots, appears around 1600 BC; by 1550 BC Mycenae dominates Achaea.
ev.olmec-rubber.n: The rubber balls of El Manatí
ev.olmec-rubber.t: A dozen rubber balls from the Olmec spring of El Manatí date to 1600 BC or earlier, made from latex mixed with the juice of a vine. They are older than the first known ballcourt, at Paso de la Amada around 1400 BC.
ev.venus-tablet.t: Babylonian astronomers record the appearances of Venus over 21 years on the Venus tablet of Ammisaduqa.
ev.hittites-babylon-1595.t: The Hittite king Mursili I sacks Babylon in 1595 BC. The First Dynasty of Babylon, Hammurabi’s, ends and the Kassites take Babylonia.
ev.new-kingdom-1550.t: Ahmose I is crowned around 1550 BC and founds the 18th dynasty; the New Kingdom of Egypt begins.
ev.egypt-nubia-1504.t: Egypt conquers Nubia and the Levant in 1504–1492 BC.
ev.kaali.t: A meteorite strikes Saaremaa in Estonia around 1500 BC and forms the Kaali crater.
ev.maya-cuello.t: The early traces of Maya civilisation, in Belize, date from around 1500 BC; the earliest traces of the Olmec are of the same century.
ev.rig-veda.t: The early hymns of the Rigveda are dated by many scholars to around 1500 BC, in the Punjab.
ev.zoroaster.t: One tradition puts the birth of Zoroaster, the prophet of the Iranian faith, around 1500 BC.
ev.megiddo-1469.t: Hatshepsut is succeeded by Thutmose III around 1480 BC, and Egypt reaches its greatest extent; around 1469 BC he defeats the Canaanites at Megiddo.
ev.ao-walls.t: The Shang capital at Ao is walled in the fifteenth century BC with ramparts about 20 m wide at the base.
ev.crete-1420.t: Mycenaeans conquer Crete around 1420 BC; the first Linear B tablets are written and the Palace of Minos burns around 1400 BC.
ev.ballcourt-1400.t: The ballcourt of Paso de la Amada is built around 1400 BC; the Olmec rubber balls of El Manatí are older still.
ev.ugarit-1400.t: Ugarit on the Syrian coast is at its height from about 1400 to 1250 BC; its texts attest a written alphabet.
ev.suppiluliuma.t: Šuppiluliuma I leads the Hittite Empire to its peak around 1380–1336 BC and conquers the weakened Mitanni; Assyria frees itself under Ashur-uballit I.
ev.amarna.t: Akhenaten builds a new capital, Akhetaten, at Amarna in 1372–1350 BC. Tutankhamun dies around 1325 BC and is buried in the Valley of the Kings.
ev.san-lorenzo-1350.t: Large public buildings are raised at San Lorenzo in Mexico between 1350 and 1250 BC.
ev.steppe-riders.t: Between about 1350 and 1250 BC pastoral nomadism develops on the Central Asian steppes, with cattle herded on horseback.
ev.uluburun.t: A merchant ship sinks off Uluburun, south of Kaş, around 1320–1295 BC, carrying the trade of the Late Bronze Age Mediterranean.
ev.abu-simbel.t: The pharaohs of the 19th dynasty complete their temples at Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel in the thirteenth century BC.
ev.mycenae-lion-gate.t: The Lion Gate and the Treasury of Atreus are built at Mycenae in the thirteenth century BC, and the palace scribes of Pylos write Linear B.
ev.shang-anyang.t: Around 1300 BC the Shang settle their capital at Yin, Anyang, where they flourish until 1046 BC. Their armies are organised in companies of a hundred men and sections of five chariots.
ev.ten-kings.n: The Battle of the Ten Kings
ev.ten-kings.t: Around 1300 BC, by the Rigveda, King Sudas defeats a coalition of ten kings in the north-west of India.
ev.tollense.n: The battle in the Tollense valley
ev.tollense.t: Some 4,000 men fight at a causeway over the Tollense in northern Germany in the thirteenth century BC, the largest known prehistoric battle north of the Alps.
ev.kadesh-1274.t: Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittites fight at Kadesh on the Orontes in 1274 BC; neither wins outright, and both sides lose heavily.
ev.lapita-1260.t: Lapita pottery at Bourewa, on the south-west coast of Viti Levu in Fiji, is dated to about 1260 BC: the seafarers of the Lapita culture have crossed the open sea to Fiji.
ev.urnfield.t: From about 1250 BC the Urnfield culture, burning its dead and burying the ashes in urns, marks the Late Bronze Age of central and western Europe.
ev.bronze-age-collapse.t: Between about 1200 and 1150 BC the palace states of Greece, Anatolia and the Levant fall and the trade of the eastern Mediterranean breaks down.
ev.gadir-1104.n: The Phoenicians in the far west
ev.gadir-1104.t: The Phoenicians found a port at Lisbon around 1200 BC and Gadir, Cádiz, around 1104 BC, beyond the Pillars of Hercules.
ev.olmec-san-lorenzo.t: The Olmec civilisation develops on the Gulf coast of Mexico around 1200 BC, with its first great centre at San Lorenzo until about 900 BC. Its seventeen known colossal heads, thought to be rulers, weigh up to an estimated 25–55 tonnes; the best jade comes from the Motagua valley of Guatemala.
ev.sea-peoples.t: Around 1200 BC bands of migrants and raiders, most of them moving by land with their families, broke over the eastern Mediterranean: Hatti, Ugarit, Ascalon and Hazor were destroyed and Cyprus was cut off. Merneptah fought them in his fifth year; Ramesses III ambushed their fleet at the mouths of the Nile in his eighth year, about 1175 BC. The Peleset settled the coast as the Philistines.
ev.troy-1184.t: Greek tradition dates the fall of Troy to the Mycenaeans to 24 April 1184 BC, after a ten-year war that legend begins around 1194 BC.
ev.hattusa-1180.t: Hittite power collapses around 1180 BC and Hattusa is destroyed; the last Kassite king of Babylon falls to the Elamites the same year.
ev.ramesses-iii-1177.n: Ramesses III and the Sea Peoples
ev.ramesses-iii-1177.t: In the eighth year of his reign, about 1177 BC, Ramesses III repels the Sea Peoples from Egypt.
ev.ramesses-v-1160.t: Pharaoh Ramesses V dies of smallpox in 1160 BC.
ev.hekla-1159.t: The Hekla 3 eruption in Iceland in 1159 BC triggers eighteen years of cooling.
ev.cascajal.t: The Cascajal block, of about 1100–900 BC, carries 62 signs, 28 of them distinct, and may be writing; many scholars doubt it because it was found out of context.
ev.dark-age-1100.t: Around 1100 BC Mycenaean civilisation ends and the Greek Dark Ages begin; the Dorians are supposed to invade.
ev.kenya-farming.t: The earliest evidence of farming in the highlands of Kenya dates from the eleventh century BC.
ev.egypt-divided-1069.t: Ramesses XI dies in 1069 BC and the 20th dynasty ends; Smendes founds the 21st.
ev.five-planets-1059.t: The Bamboo Annals record five planets gathering in the evening sky in May 1059 BC, thirteen years before the Zhou overthrow the Shang.
ev.phoenician-alphabet.t: The Phoenician alphabet is invented in the eleventh century BC, about when the Latins arrive in Italy.
ev.zhou.t: About 1046 BC the Zhou defeat the last Shang king and rule from the Wei valley.
ev.saul-1026.t: Saul becomes the first king of the Israelites around 1026 BC; David succeeds around 1010 BC.
ev.aramaic.t: The earliest extant written Aramaic dates from the late tenth century BC; around 500 BC Darius I makes Aramaic the official language of the western Persian Empire.
ev.golden-hats.t: Bronze Age goldsmiths of Central Europe make the ceremonial golden hats in the late tenth century BC.
ev.iron-india-1000.n: The Iron Age kingdoms of India
ev.iron-india-1000.t: Around 1000 BC Iron Age kingdoms rule northern and southern India: Kuru, Panchala, Kosala, Videha and the Pandya.
ev.latins-1000.t: The Latins arrive in Italy around 1000 BC, in the age of the Villanovan culture.
ev.sa-huynh.t: The Sa Huỳnh culture begins in central and southern Vietnam around 1000 BC.
ev.first-temple-957.t: David, king of the united monarchy of Israel, dies around 965 BC. By tradition Solomon completes the First Temple in Jerusalem in 957 BC; after his death in 931 BC the kingdom splits into Judah and Israel.
ev.sparta-950.t: Sparta is founded late in the tenth century BC, in Greece’s dark age; the Lefkandi centaur is made on Euboea.
ev.shoshenq-943.t: Shoshenq I founds Egypt’s 22nd dynasty around 943 BC, at the end of the 21st.
ev.anuradhapura-900.t: Anuradhapura is founded in Sri Lanka around 900 BC; in northern Italy the Villanovan culture emerges.
ev.chavin.t: The Chavín culture of the Peruvian Andes develops around 900 BC around its temple at Chavín de Huántar, built in at least fifteen phases; at its heart stands the Lanzón, a carved granite shaft 4.53 m tall showing a fanged god. Chavín style spreads from Piura to Paracas before the culture ends around 250 BC.
ev.olmec-la-venta.n: La Venta and the Olmec pyramids
ev.olmec-la-venta.t: La Venta is the main Olmec centre from about 900 to 400 BC, with its Great Pyramid; around 800 BC the Olmecs are building pyramids. In the north-eastern woodlands of North America the Adena culture appears.
ev.nimrud-880.t: Ashurnasirpal II becomes king of Assyria in 884 BC and moves his capital to Nimrud around 880 BC.
ev.urartu-860.t: The kingdom of Urartu is unified around 860 BC in the Armenian highlands; Argishti I founds Erebuni, today’s Yerevan, in 782 BC.
ev.qarqar-853.t: Shalmaneser III of Assyria fights a coalition led by Damascus at Qarqar on the Orontes in 854 or 853 BC, without a decision; in 842 BC he devastates Damascus and Israel and the Phoenician cities pay him tribute.
ev.tagaung-850.t: By tradition Abhiyaza founds the Tagaung kingdom on the Irrawaddy in northern Burma around 850 BC.
ev.phoenicians.t: Settlers from Tyre founded Carthage in 814–813 BC, a date that radiocarbon puts at 835–800 BC; Gadir, Motya and the other western stations followed the silver and tin routes to Iberia. The Phoenician trading-posts became the Carthaginian empire.
ev.gonghe-841.n: The first year of Chinese annual dating
ev.gonghe-841.t: King Li of Zhou is driven into exile in 841 BC; from that year Chinese history is dated year by year without a break.
ev.carthage-founded.t: Phoenicians from Tyre found Carthage in 814 BC.
ev.hallstatt-800.t: Around 800 BC the Iron Age and the Hallstatt culture spread through Central Europe with the Proto-Celtic language; the Etruscan civilisation emerges in Italy.
ev.greek-colonisation.t: From about 800 BC Greek cities planted colonies in two waves, in the early eighth and in the sixth century BC: Pithecusae about 800, Syracuse and Naxos about 734, Sinope 756, Cyrene 632/31, Massalia about 598, Emporion in the early sixth century. Miletus alone founded more than 60 colonies, and more than thirty cities had several.
ev.celts.t: From the Hallstatt lands north of the Alps (c. 800–500 BC) and the La Tène culture (from about 450 BC) Celtic peoples spread into Gaul, Iberia, Britain and Ireland. In 391 BC Celts seized the Po valley; the Senones sacked Rome in 390 BC; the Scordisci took Singidunum in the third century and other bands crossed into Anatolia as the Galatians.
ev.sungai-batu-788.n: The iron port of Sungai Batu
ev.sungai-batu-788.t: A port and iron-working centre is founded at Sungai Batu in Kedah on the Malay Peninsula around 788 BC.
ev.olympics-776.t: The first recorded games are held at Olympia in 776 BC.
ev.zhou-east-771.t: Hao is sacked in 771 BC and King You is killed; the Western Zhou ends and the court moves east to Chengzhou in 770 BC. The Spring and Autumn period begins in 722 BC.
ev.rome-founded.t: Rome is founded in 753 BC by the traditional reckoning.
ev.homer.t: The Iliad and the Odyssey are dated to 750–650 BC, the age of the first Olympiads and the Greek alphabet.
ev.assyria-745.t: Tiglath-Pileser III takes the Assyrian throne in 745 BC and makes Israel pay tribute. Sargon II conquers the kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and founds a new capital at Dur-Sharrukin in 717 BC.
ev.syracuse-734.t: Corinth founds Syracuse in Sicily in 734 BC and Sparta founds Taras in 706 BC; the Greek colonies of the west begin.
ev.piye-728.t: Piye, king of Kush at Napata since about 730 BC, invades Egypt in 728 BC, takes Memphis and founds the 25th dynasty.
ev.upanishads.t: The Upanishads are composed in India around 700 BC. On the Pontic steppe the Scythians begin to settle the lands of the Cimmerians.
ev.dmt-690.t: An inscription of the 690s BC from D’mt in Ethiopia names Karib’il Watar, king of Saba in Arabia, across the Red Sea.
ev.taharqa-690.t: Taharqa of Kush takes the Egyptian throne around 690 BC, one of the Nubian pharaohs of the 25th dynasty; his sphinx is carved at Kawa. He holds off the first Assyrian invasion in 674 BC.
ev.assyria-egypt-671.t: Esarhaddon invades Egypt in 671 BC and takes Memphis; Ashurbanipal sacks Thebes in 664 BC. Psamtik I drives the Assyrians out and by 656 BC rules all Egypt; the Kushite dynasty ends.
ev.ashurbanipal-library.t: Nineveh becomes the largest city in the world in 668 BC. In the 640s BC Ashurbanipal founds there the library that keeps the earliest complete copy of the Epic of Gilgamesh.
ev.byzantium-667.t: By tradition colonists from Megara under Byzas found Byzantium on the Bosporus in 667 BC, the century of Greek colonies from Abdera to Cyrene.
ev.jimmu-660.t: Japanese tradition dates the founding of the country by Emperor Jimmu to 11 February 660 BC.
ev.lydian-coins.t: The Lydians of western Anatolia strike the first metal coins in the seventh century BC; the timeline of inventions puts coinage at about 600 BC, in Lydia or Phoenicia.
ev.zapotec.t: The Zapotec civilisation begins to develop in the Valley of Oaxaca in the seventh century BC. In the Maya lowlands Piedras Negras is first occupied in the 650s BC.
ev.cyrene-631.t: Greek colonists found Cyrene in Libya around 631 BC.
ev.nineveh-612.t: Babylonians, Medes and Scythians destroy Nineveh in 612 BC and the Assyrian empire ends.
ev.carchemish-605.t: Necho II of Egypt kills Josiah of Judah at Megiddo in 609 BC; at Carchemish in 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar defeats Necho.
ev.mahajanapadas-600.n: The sixteen great states of India
ev.mahajanapadas-600.t: Around 600 BC sixteen Mahajanapadas, the great realms, rule northern India. Pataliputra is established as a capital of Magadha around 500 BC, and Vaishali is counted the first republic.
ev.massalia-600.t: Greeks from Phocaea found Massalia, Marseille, around 600 BC; Celts found Milan about the same time.
ev.cleisthenes-507.t: Solon reforms the laws of Athens in 594 BC. The tyrant Hippias is expelled in 510 BC and Cleisthenes’ reforms of 507–501 BC found the Athenian democracy.
ev.meroe-590.t: An Egyptian army sacks Napata in 590 BC and the Kushite court moves south to Meroë on the Nile.
ev.babylonian-exile.n: The Temple destroyed and the exile
ev.babylonian-exile.t: Babylon takes Jerusalem in 597 BC and again in 587 BC; Solomon’s Temple is destroyed and the Babylonian captivity begins. After Cyrus takes Babylon the exiles may return, and the Second Temple is completed on 12 March 515 BC.
ev.thales-585.t: Thales of Miletus predicts the solar eclipse of 28 May 585 BC, which halts a battle between the Lydians and the Medes. Pythagoras is born on Samos around 570 BC.
ev.buddha-life.n: The Buddha teaches in the Ganges plain
ev.buddha-life.t: Siddhartha Gautama, born about 563 BC by the traditional count, teaches in the Ganges plain and dies about 483 BC.
ev.persian-empire-550.t: Cyrus II overthrows Astyages of Media in 553–550 BC and founds the Persian Empire. He defeats Croesus near the Halys and completes the conquest of Lydia in 546 BC, with Pasargadae his capital.
ev.confucius.t: Confucius is born in 551 BC and dies in 479 BC; a temple to him is founded at Qufu the next year.
ev.carthage-west-550.t: Carthage conquers Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica in the 550s BC and takes Gadir around 501 BC.
ev.cyrus-babylon.t: Cyrus the Great takes Babylon in 539 BC, ends the Neo-Babylonian empire and frees the Jewish exiles.
ev.cambyses-525.t: Cambyses II conquers Egypt in 525 BC; Darius I completes the occupation of the Punjab in 516 BC and makes Aramaic the official language of the western empire.
ev.roman-republic.t: Tarquin the Proud is expelled and the Republic founded in 509 BC.
ev.boju-506.t: The state of Wu, with Sun Tzu, defeats Chu at Boju in 506 BC.
ev.marathon.t: The Greek cities defeat the Persian landing at Marathon in 490 BC.
ev.buddha-death-483.t: The Buddha dies around 483 BC; the First Buddhist Council meets at Rajgaha.
ev.grand-canal-486.t: The first part of the Grand Canal of China is dug in 486 BC.
ev.xerxes-480.t: Xerxes crosses the Hellespont in 480 BC, forces Thermopylae and burns Athens, but his fleet is beaten at Salamis.
ev.himera-480.t: In 480 BC, the year of Salamis, the Greeks of Sicily defeat the Carthaginians at Himera.
ev.parthenon-447.t: The Parthenon is begun in 447 BC and completed in 438 BC. Herodotus finishes his Histories around 449 BC and Aeschylus the Oresteia in 458 BC; Rome publishes the Twelve Tables in 449 BC.
ev.democritus-440.t: Democritus proposes around 440 BC that matter is made of indivisible particles, atoms. Hippocrates had been born on Kos around 460 BC.
ev.peloponnesian-war.t: Athens and Sparta fight from 431 to 404 BC; Athens loses.
ev.plague-athens.t: Thucydides says the sickness came out of Ethiopia through Egypt and Libya and first appeared at Athens in the port of Piraeus, in 430 BC, brought by ships. It returned in 429 and again in the winter of 427/426. Pericles died in 429, by Plutarch’s account.
ev.jomon-ends.t: The Jōmon period of Japan ends around 400 BC.
ev.socrates-399.t: Athens sentences Socrates to death in 399 BC. His pupil Plato founds the Academy in Athens in 387 BC, where mathematics, astronomy and philosophy are taught.
ev.allia-387.t: Gauls under Brennus defeat the Romans at the Allia in 387 BC, nine years after Camillus destroyed Veii.
ev.buddhist-council-383.t: The Second Buddhist Council meets at Vaisali around 383 BC.
ev.shang-yang-356.t: Shang Yang begins his reforms of the state of Qin in 356 BC.
ev.alexander.t: Alexander crosses to Asia in 334 BC, wins at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, takes Egypt, Persia and Bactria, turns back at the Hyphasis in 326 and dies in Babylon in June 323 BC.
ev.gaugamela-331.t: Alexander defeats Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BC and ends Persian hegemony. He beats Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BC and dies at Babylon in 323 BC, where his generals divide the conquests.
ev.maurya-founded.t: Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nanda dynasty of Magadha in 321 BC.
ev.library-alexandria.t: Ptolemy founds the Museum and Library of Alexandria around 307 BC, with about a hundred scholars. The Pharos is completed there around 285 BC.
ev.seleucus-maurya-304.t: Chandragupta Maurya defeats Seleucus I around 304 BC; in the settlement he gives Seleucus 500 war elephants.
ev.pyrrhus-280.t: Pyrrhus of Epirus invades Italy in 280 BC, the year the Colossus of Rhodes is completed.
ev.ashoka-edicts-260.t: Ashoka rules the Mauryan Empire from about 273 to 232 BC. After the Kalinga war he has his edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars across India.
ev.first-punic-264.t: Rome and Carthage go to war over Sicily in 264 BC; the war ends in Carthage’s defeat in 241 BC.
ev.kalinga.t: Ashoka conquers Kalinga in 261 BC and afterwards sends Buddhist missions abroad, to Sri Lanka among others.
ev.changping-260.t: Qin defeats Zhao at Changping in 260 BC. Between 225 and 222 BC Qin conquers Wei, Chu, Yan and Zhao.
ev.au-lac-257.t: An Dương Vương overthrows the Hồng Bàng dynasty in Vietnam in 258–257 BC; Zhao Tuo defeats him in 208 BC and founds the Triệu dynasty of Nanyue.
ev.dujiangyan-256.t: Li Bing builds the Dujiangyan irrigation system on the Min river in Sichuan in 256 BC.
ev.qin-unification.t: Qin Shi Huang conquers the other warring states and takes the title of emperor in 221 BC.
ev.hannibal.t: Hannibal leaves New Carthage in 218 BC, crosses the Rhône and the Alps with fewer than 35,000 men left, wins in Italy and is beaten by Scipio at Zama in 202 BC.
ev.cannae-216.t: Two years after crossing the Alps, Hannibal destroys a Roman army at Cannae in 216 BC.
ev.great-wall-214.t: Qin Shi Huang, who has unified China in 221 BC, orders the building of the Great Wall against the northern nomads in 214 BC. He dies in 210 BC and his dynasty falls in 206 BC.
ev.han-founded.t: The Han are established in 206 BC; trade links with the West open along what becomes the Silk Road.
ev.zama-202.t: The Romans defeat Carthage in Africa in 202 BC and end the Second Punic War. In China Liu Bang founds the Han dynasty the same year.
ev.baideng-200.t: The Xiongnu of the steppe defeat the new Han dynasty at Baideng in 200 BC.
ev.barangay-200.t: Around 200 BC the barangay polities begin to form in the Philippines.
ev.eratosthenes-200.t: Eratosthenes of Alexandria calculates the circumference of the Earth around 200 BC.
ev.paper-han.t: Paper is first made in Han China in the second century BC; Cai Lun’s improved paper follows in AD 105.
ev.magnesia-190.t: Rome defeats Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC, Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC and Perseus at Pydna in 168 BC; the Antigonid kingdom is dissolved.
ev.rosetta-196.t: Ptolemy V is crowned at Memphis in 196 BC, aged fourteen, and the priests issue the decree that is carved on the Rosetta Stone.
ev.shunga-185.t: Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last Maurya emperor in 185 BC and founds the Shunga dynasty.
ev.yuezhi-176.t: The Xiongnu defeat the Yuezhi around 176 BC and the Yuezhi migrate west from Gansu to the Ili valley; the Wusun drive them out of the Ili around 160 BC.
ev.maccabees-164.t: Judas Maccabaeus restores the Temple in Jerusalem on 25 Kislev 164 BC.
ev.carthage-destroyed.t: The Third Punic War ends with the destruction of Carthage in 146 BC.
ev.corinth-146.t: In 146 BC, the year it destroys Carthage, Rome razes Corinth and dissolves the Achaean League; Greece is Rome’s.
ev.han-wudi-141.t: Emperor Wu begins a reign of 54 years in 141 BC. From the ambush at Mayi in 133 BC the Han make war on the Xiongnu.
ev.numantia-133.t: Scipio Aemilianus takes Numantia in Spain in 133 BC.
ev.hipparchus-130.t: Hipparchus compiles a large star catalogue around 130 BC and calculates the precession of the equinoxes.
ev.teotihuacan.t: Teotihuacan is founded in the Valley of Mexico around 100 BC, and the Pyramid of the Sun is complete by about AD 100. At its height around 450 the city covers some 30 km² and may hold 150,000 people; its great monuments are sacked and burned around 550. The Aztecs, who found it in ruins, give it its name.
ev.asiatic-vespers-88.t: Mithridates VI of Pontus has the Romans and Italians of Asia Minor massacred in 88 BC; 80,000 are killed. Rome’s Mithridatic wars end only with his suicide in 63 BC.
ev.sulla-82.t: In 88 BC Sulla becomes the first Roman general to march on Rome; he does it again in 83 BC and is made dictator in 81 BC.
ev.spartacus-73.t: Spartacus leads the slave revolt of the Third Servile War from 73 BC; Pompey and Crassus end it in 71 BC.
ev.pompey-east-63.t: Pompey clears the Mediterranean of pirates in forty days in 67 BC, drives Mithridates out of Asia Minor and takes Jerusalem in 63 BC.
ev.caesar-gaul.t: Caesar beats the Helvetii at Bibracte in 58 BC and the Belgae at the Sabis in 57, destroys the Veneti fleet in 56, bridges the Rhine and lands in Britain in 55 and 54, and takes Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BC.
ev.silla-57.t: By tradition the Korean kingdom of Silla is founded in 57 BC.
ev.carrhae-53.t: The Parthians destroy the army of Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC.
ev.caesar-civil-war.t: Caesar crosses the Rubicon in January 49 BC, rules as dictator and is murdered on 15 March 44 BC.
ev.maya-zero.t: A Maya numeral for zero is written at Chiapa in 36 BC.
ev.actium.t: Octavian's fleet defeats Antony and Cleopatra off Actium in 31 BC.
ev.augustus-principate.t: Octavian receives the title Augustus in 27 BC and rules until his death in AD 14.
ev.han-census-2.t: The Han census completed in AD 2 counts 59,594,978 people.
ev.teutoburg.n: The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
ev.teutoburg.t: Arminius destroys three Roman legions in AD 9.
ev.wang-mang-9.t: Wang Mang deposes the Han child-emperor in AD 9 and founds the Xin dynasty; the Eastern Han is established in 25.
ev.crucifixion.t: Jesus is crucified at Jerusalem between AD 30 and 33; the exact year is unknown.
ev.trung-sisters-40.t: The Trưng sisters lead the Vietnamese against Han rule in 40–43; the rising is put down.
ev.paul-journeys.t: Paul's journeys of about 45–57 carry the new faith from Antioch through Cyprus and Anatolia to Macedonia, Athens, Corinth and Ephesus.
ev.boudica-60.t: Boudica of the Iceni rises against Roman rule in Britain in 60.
ev.peter-64.t: The Great Fire of Rome in 64 destroys two-thirds of the city and Nero’s persecution of the Christians begins. Tradition holds that Peter, counted the first bishop of Rome, is crucified under Nero between 64 and 68 and buried on the Vatican Hill, where Constantine later builds the basilica over his grave.
ev.buddhism-china.t: Buddhism comes to China in 67 with the monks Kasyapa and Dharmaraksha; the White Horse Temple is founded at Luoyang in 68.
ev.four-emperors-69.n: The Year of the Four Emperors
ev.four-emperors-69.t: Four emperors claim Rome in 69 and Vespasian wins. Jerusalem is sacked and the Second Temple destroyed in 70; Masada falls in 73.
ev.jerusalem-70.t: Titus's armies destroy Jerusalem and its Temple in AD 70.
ev.xiongnu-91.n: The Han defeat the Northern Xiongnu
ev.xiongnu-91.t: Han armies defeat the Northern Xiongnu at Yiwulu in 73 and in the Altai in 89; the war ends in the Ili valley in 91.
ev.codex-100.t: The codex, the bound book of leaves, appears in the Roman Empire around 100. In China Wang Chong describes a chain pump around 80.
ev.grand-anicut.t: A Chola king builds the Grand Anicut dam across the Kaveri in the second century.
ev.hindu-numerals.t: Between the first and sixth centuries the Hindu number system develops in the Indian subcontinent, the decimal numerals the world now writes.
ev.moche.t: The Moche culture develops on the north coast of Peru around AD 100, while Teotihuacan grows to 60,000–80,000 people.
ev.cai-lun-105.t: Cai Lun makes modern paper in Han China in 105. Earlier forms of paper had been made there since the second century BC.
ev.trajan-extent.t: Under Trajan, from the conquest of Dacia to 117, the Roman Empire reaches its largest extent.
ev.hadrians-wall.t: Work on Hadrian's Wall begins in 122.
ev.zhang-heng-132.t: Zhang Heng builds a water-powered armillary sphere in 125 and a seismometer in 132 at the Han capital.
ev.kanishka-127.t: Kanishka rules the Kushan Empire across Pakistan and northern India from about 127 to 140. Gandhara’s sculptors carve the Buddha in human form in the second or third century.
ev.bar-kokhba-132.t: Simon bar Kokhba leads the Jews of Judea in revolt against Rome in 132–135, while Hadrian’s Wall is being built in Britain.
ev.antonine-wall-142.t: Rome builds the Antonine Wall across central Scotland in 142–154, north of Hadrian’s Wall.
ev.antonine-plague.t: Soldiers of Lucius Verus’s Parthian campaign probably carried the sickness home from the siege of Seleucia in the winter of 165–166; the first documented case was at Smyrna in 165. Galen described its fever, diarrhoea and rash. It reached Rome in 166, the Rhine legions and Gaul, and nearly every part of the empire by 172.
ev.marcomannic-166.t: Marcus Aurelius fights the Marcomannic Wars on the Danube frontier from 166 to 180, in the years of the Antonine Plague.
ev.yellow-turbans-184.t: The Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 breaks the Han; warlords fight over the court and Cao Cao defeats Yuan Shao at Guandu in 200.
ev.red-cliffs-208.t: Cao Cao is defeated at the Red Cliffs on the Yangtze in 208. When the Han ends in 220, China divides into the Three Kingdoms.
ev.antoniniana-212.t: Caracalla’s Constitutio Antoniniana of 212 grants Roman citizenship to the free people of the empire; the Baths of Caracalla rise in Rome.
ev.han-ends.t: The Han dynasty falls in 220 and the Three Kingdoms period begins.
ev.sasanians-224.t: Ardashir I defeats the last Parthian king, Artabanus V, at Hormozdgan in 224 and Sasanian rule over Persia begins. In 260 Shapur I captures the Roman emperor Valerian.
ev.crisis-235.n: The Crisis of the Third Century
ev.crisis-235.t: From 235 to 284 the Roman Empire passes through about fifty years of civil war, invasion and no fewer than twenty emperors, until Diocletian.
ev.mani-242.t: Mani preaches his new faith, Manichaeism, at the Sasanian court from 242 to 274.
ev.plague-cyprian.t: Contemporaries said it came out of Ethiopia. Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote of it in Egypt around Easter 249, and it reached Rome by the second half of 251 at the latest. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, whose name it carries, and his biographer Pontius described the dying in Carthage.
ev.maya-classic-cities.t: The Classic period of the Maya begins around AD 250. Tikal and Calakmul are the great rivals; the largest cities hold 50,000 to 120,000 people, and Tikal covers about 20 km².
ev.goths.n: The Goths and the Migration Period
ev.goths.t: Fleeing the Huns, the Tervingi crossed the Danube in 376 and destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378; Alaric’s Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, settled in Gaul and founded a kingdom in Iberia about 460. The Rhine crossing of 406, Theodoric’s Ostrogoths in Italy in 489 and the Lombards in 568 closed the age; Odoacer deposed the last western emperor in 476.
ev.jin-280.t: Sima Yan founds the Jin dynasty in 266 and reunites China in 280 by conquering Eastern Wu.
ev.tetrarchy-293.t: Diocletian reigns from 284 to 305 and in 293 divides the rule of the empire among four emperors, the Tetrarchy.
ev.kofun.t: The Kofun era of great keyhole-shaped tombs begins in Japan around 300 and lasts until 538.
ev.armenia-301.t: Armenia becomes the first kingdom to make Christianity its state religion, in 301.
ev.jin-south-317.t: The Sixteen Kingdoms period begins in northern China in 304, and around 317 the Jin court retreats south of the Yangtze; the Eastern Jin rules from Jiankang.
ev.milan-313.t: Constantine and Licinius grant toleration to Christians in 313.
ev.butuan-boat-320.t: Butuan Boat One is built in the Philippines around 320.
ev.gupta-320.t: The Gupta Empire is established in northern India early in the fourth century, and Samudragupta expands it in 335–380.
ev.stirrup-322.t: The stirrup is invented in China no later than 322.
ev.nicaea-325.t: The first ecumenical council meets at Nicaea in 325.
ev.aksum-christian.t: The kingdom of Aksum declares Christianity its state religion under King Ezana; the timeline dates it to 325.
ev.constantinople-330.t: Constantine names his new capital on the Bosporus in 330.
ev.aksum-kush-350.t: Around 350 the Kingdom of Aksum conquers the Kingdom of Kush on the middle Nile, twenty years after Aksum adopts Christianity.
ev.mulavarman-350.t: The Mulavarman inscription of eastern Borneo, around 350, is the earliest in Indonesia.
ev.crete-365.t: An earthquake of magnitude at least eight and a tsunami strike the eastern Mediterranean in 365.
ev.huns.t: The Huns reached the Volga by 370 and in the 370s conquered the Alans and most of the Goths, who fled across the Danube. By the 420s they held the Hungarian plain; Attila invaded Gaul in 451 and Italy in 452 and died in 453. Their empire broke at the Nedao about 454.
ev.adrianople-378.t: The Goths destroy the eastern army and kill the emperor Valens in 378.
ev.tikal-378.t: In January 378 Siyaj K’ak’, a lord tied to Teotihuacan, conquers Waka, Tikal and Uaxactun and replaces the king of Tikal.
ev.thessalonica-380.t: Theodosius makes Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire in 380.
ev.gupta-golden-age.t: Chandragupta II’s reign of about 380–415 is the golden age of the Gupta Empire of northern India. Skandagupta, the last great Gupta emperor, rules until 467.
ev.fei-383.t: The Eastern Jin defeat Fu Jian’s invasion at the Fei river in 383.
ev.empire-split-395.t: Theodosius I dies in 395 and the Roman Empire splits permanently into East and West. He had banned pagan worship and the First Council of Constantinople had reaffirmed the Trinity in 381.
ev.faxian-399.t: The Chinese monk Faxian leaves for India in 399 to gather Buddhist texts. He travels through India and Sri Lanka and is home by 412.
ev.armenian-alphabet-405.t: Mesrop Mashtots introduces the Armenian alphabet in 405; 36 of its 38 letters are his.
ev.vandals.t: The Vandals crossed the Rhine on 31 December 405, the Pyrenees on 13 October 409, and under Gaiseric the strait to Africa in 429. They took Carthage on 19 October 439 and sacked Rome in 455; the kingdom ended with Gelimer’s surrender in 534.
ev.anglo-saxons.t: Germanic soldiers served in Britain in the fourth century; larger numbers came in the early fifth, after the end of Roman rule in 411, from Old Saxony, Jutland, Angeln and Frisia. Estimates of the migrants run from 20,000 to 200,000 into a population of perhaps one to four million.
ev.city-of-god-413.t: Three years after the sack of Rome, Augustine begins The City of God at Hippo in 413.
ev.copan-426.t: K’inich Yax K’uk’ Mo’ re-establishes Copán in 426. At Tikal the North Acropolis is built in the fifth century.
ev.ilopango-430.t: The Ilopango volcano in El Salvador erupts around 430 and devastates the nearby Maya cities.
ev.patrick-432.t: St Patrick begins his mission in Ireland in 432.
ev.vandals-rome-455.t: The Vandals conquer Carthage in 439 and sack Rome in 455.
ev.hopewell-end.t: The Hopewell tradition of the Ohio and Mississippi valleys comes to an end in the fifth century.
ev.slavs.t: The Slavs appear in Byzantine records in the early sixth century; Procopius (545) and Jordanes (551) describe them on the Danube. Between 500 and 700 they settled between the Oder and the Elbe, Bohemia and Pannonia, the eastern Alps and the Balkans down to the Peloponnese, and spread north along the upper Dnieper. Their homeland is best placed in southern Belarus and northern Ukraine.
ev.catalaunian-451.t: Romans and Visigoths defeat Attila’s Huns on the Catalaunian Plains in 451. Attila destroys Aquileia the next year, is turned from Rome by Pope Leo I and dies in 453; his empire falls apart after Nedao in 454.
ev.chalcedon-451.t: The fourth ecumenical council meets at Chalcedon in 451, the year of the Catalaunian Plains. Ephesus had upheld the title Theotokos for Mary in 431.
ev.rome-falls-476.n: The end of the Western Empire
ev.rome-falls-476.t: Odoacer forces Romulus Augustulus to abdicate in 476.
ev.theodoric-493.t: Theodoric the Ostrogoth ousts Odoacer and becomes king of Italy in 493.
ev.shaolin-495.t: The Shaolin Monastery is founded on Mount Song in 477 or 495, in the age of the Northern and Southern dynasties.
ev.clovis-496.t: Clovis, king of the Franks, is baptised at Reims in 496.
ev.wari.t: From about AD 500 the Wari state, ruled from Huari near Ayacucho, spreads over much of the Peruvian highlands and coast. Its records are kept on knotted khipu, perhaps first used here, and its sites lie along the later Inca roads; drought weakens it from about 800 and Huari is largely empty by 1000.
ev.madagascar.t: Between the fifth and seventh centuries Austronesian voyagers from the Borneo region crossed the whole Indian Ocean to settle Madagascar, 7,000 km from home. Malagasy is still a language of the Barito family of Borneo.
ev.silk-522.t: The Romans obtain silkworm eggs around 522 and begin to raise silk in the Eastern Empire.
ev.anno-domini-525.t: Dionysius Exiguus devises the Anno Domini system of counting years at Rome in 525.
ev.monte-cassino-529.t: Benedict of Nursia founds the monastery of Monte Cassino in 529. Boethius had written The Consolation of Philosophy in prison around 524.
ev.nika-532.t: In the Nika riots at Constantinople in 532 the cathedral is destroyed and up to 30,000 people are killed.
ev.justinian-reconquest.t: Belisarius retakes North Africa from the Vandals in 533; the Gothic War of 535–554 brings Italy back under Constantinople at great cost.
ev.buddhism-japan.t: Buddhism is introduced to Japan from Baekje in 538 or 552.
ev.plague-justinian.t: Procopius first reports the plague at Pelusium, near Suez, in 541. Grain ships from Egypt carried it to Constantinople in 542, where Justinian fell ill and recovered, and by 543 it had reached every corner of his empire. Burials at Edix Hill near Cambridge show it in Britain, and it returned in waves until about 750.
ev.nubia-christian.t: Nobatia converts to Christianity in 545, and Alodia and Makuria in 569.
